overall_summary: Analysis of the deduplicated performance data clearly highlights that 'What If' scenarios and extreme space phenomena (specifically exotic planets and hypothetical physics interactions) dramatically outperform standard trivia facts in views-per-day, likes-per-view, and overall engagement. Videos featuring immersive thought experiments like falling into extreme alien worlds (e.g., liquid diamond planets or burning ice worlds) consistently drive higher interaction rates than straightforward historical or psychological trivia.

winning_patterns.evidence: Videos like 'What If You Fell Into a Liquid Diamond Planet?' (1,024 views, 38 likes) and 'What If You Fell Into the Planet of Burning Ice?' (972 views, 18 likes) show exceptionally high view velocity and engagement compared to older static fact formats.
winning_patterns.action: Double down on hypothetical immersion hooks ('What If You Fell Into...') focusing on extreme astrophysical environments.

winning_patterns.pattern: Extreme Planetary Conditions & Rare Material Rains
winning_patterns.evidence: Titles detailing bizarre planetary mechanics or extreme weather (e.g., 'The Planet Darker Than Coal: TrES-2b', 'This Planet Rains Supersonic Rubies!') generate strong baseline curiosity and high like counts.
winning_patterns.action: Produce more short-form concepts focusing on bizarre, counter-intuitive exoplanet weather and extreme physical properties.

weak_patterns.evidence: Topics like 'Your Brain Can Create Fake Memories' and general psychological tricks show low view counts (often under 60 views) and minimal likes/comments across multiple iterations.
weak_patterns.action: Deprioritize standard psychology trivia and cognitive illusion shorts unless framed within a high-stakes narrative or 'What If' scenario.

weak_patterns.evidence: General historical questions like 'The 2,000-Year-Old Mystery Science Can't Solve' generated modest views (139) with zero likes or comments, indicating low retention or weak hook resonance.
weak_patterns.action: Pivot away from abstract historical mysteries for Shorts; reserve history storytelling for deep-dive formats or cinematic micro-dramas.
